The Moors Mountain Fire, first reported on July 16th at approximately 3:45 PM near the Moors Mountains in Gates of the Mountain Wilderness, was a 98 acre wildfire caused by lightning. On July 24th, crews achieved 100% containment. More than 80 personnel worked out of spike camps in the Gates of the Mountain Wilderness, for multiple operational periods, and were supported by helicopter operations to supply the camps and to provide fire suppression. Crews utilized handlines which were tied into natural features, such as rock formations, to minimize the impact on the wilderness area.

Severe businesses sustained damage, including Helena YWCA and the Lewis and Clark Library. 1 to 2 feet of water flowing up against business doors. Flood waters up to bumpers of vans. Moviegoers at the Helena Cinemark report the movie theater being evacuated, with water draining into the lobby area. Some vehicles were also initially stranded in the lower level of the Great Northern Parking Garage. Several streets in the Capitol area saw rapid flooding with a number of homeowners reporting basement flooding.
Law enforcement closed portions of neill and fuller avenues due to flooding. Water flooded down Last Chance Gulch and impacted numerous businesses.

Extreme critical fire weather concerns on top of a quickly moving cold front bringing strong wind gusts in excess of 50 mph accelerated a grass fire in Pondera County along Highway 91, three miles north of Conrad, named the Pondera County Fire. The fire was estimated to have burned 2186 acres, destroying a family of 5's homestead and causing road closures. A collective response by the DNRC, several fire departments, Hutterite colonies within the vicinity, and local farmers and ranchers aided in the firefighting efforts.

A wildfire by the name of Eagle Creek Fire started approximately 30 miles south of Havre in the Bears Paw Mountains. An estimated 7225 acres were burned and required the usage of 173 response personnel. Lions Campground and Sandy Creek Campground were both closed during the wildfire and only emergency and local traffic were allowed on Beaver Creek Road above Upper Bear Paw Lake. The wildfire was contained around the 21st. At the time of publication, the cause of the fire was still under investigation.

The Matt Staff Road Fire was a fire that started on a Red Flag Warning Day approximately 5 miles east of East Helena, MT.  The fire quickly spread east, given strong westerly winds the day the fire started, and ultimately burned to about 12 miles east of East Helena. The fire started near Spokane Creek Road, just off U.S. Highway 12 near state Highway 284. It originally burned grassland, then crested the ridge between East Helena and Canyon Ferry Reservoir and began to burn brush. Cause of the fire has officially been listed as Unknown.

events.cz_name: GALLATIN AND MADISON COUNTY MOUNTAINS AND CENTENNIAL MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Search and Rescue teams faced difficult terrain and harsh weather while attempting a backcountry rescue in snowy and icy conditions. Details...Gallatin County 911 received a call from the Garmin International Emergency Response Coordination Center (IERCC), who had received an SOS from a satellite communication device.  After communicating with the device owner, it was determined a hunter had broken their leg while navigating rough terrain near the Albino Lake Trail in Big Sky.|Gallatin County Sheriff Search and Rescue Big Sky Section, Valley Section, and a Big Sky Fire Department responded to assist with the call. SAR Big Sky and Valley ground teams deployed on foot to the patient with ropes and a one wheeled litter. Another SAR Big Sky team deployed from the Eldridge Trailhead on a four-wheel drive side by side. Teams faced difficult terrain and harsh weather while attempting the backcountry rescue in snowy and icy conditions. It took volunteers several hours to locate, assess, and evacuate the patient. Once ground teams arrived at the patient���s location, they stabilized the injury and created a plan to evacuate the hunter by one wheeled litter, and then onto the side by side for transport back to the trailhead. The hunter was then transported several miles down the trail to the Big Sky Fire Department Ambulance and ultimately transported to Bozeman Health for further evaluation.

Multi-car pile-up reported at 16:02 at mile marker 37 on MT Highway 287 in Sheridan. Ten vehicles were involved, and a loaded school bus was stuck in the chaos. There were six ambulatory patients. Conditions were blizzard-like, with little to no visibility. The temperature with wind chill was approximately -37. Victims were escorted to a local church to speak with Montana Highway Patrol and evaluated by EMTs. Some vehicles were left in the ditches until the weather improved for them to be removed safely. Throughout the evening and the following day, there were additional slide-offs. Two minutes after the 10-car pile-up report, another incident at mile marker 1 MT Highway 84 in Norris occurred on the opposite side of the county, reported at 16:04. This incident involved two vehicles, one of which was a school vehicle carrying numerous children. No reported injuries were involved, but road and weather conditions were terrible and deteriorating quickly.

Significant snowmelt resulted in flooding along Battle Creek, near Chinook. The creek crested on April 12th at 11.94 feet. Several roads across northern and central Blaine County were impacted as a result. Water was reported over Highway 2, west of Chinook, for a time. Runoff from Cypress Hills in southern Canada may have contributed to the flooding.

Significant flooding occurred along the Milk River across Blaine County. The Rocky Boy SNOTEL station which is the main Milk River basin station peaked later than normal and had over 3.5 times the snow water equivalent that it normally would on April 6 (10.7��� of snow water equivalent versus a normal of 3.0���). When this thick snowpack melted, virtually the entire Milk River system flooded in a matter of days, as a result. The Milk River near Harlem crested at 23.80 feet on April 12, which as of this entry was the seventh highest river level recorded at this site. Roughly 4,000 aces of irrigation land was flooded. Chinook water plant was surrounded by water. Several roads and homes were impacted.

Mountain snowpack in the Milk River basin melted out very quickly and contributed significant flooding. Virtually the entire Milk River system flooded in a matter of days as a result, starting near the headwaters in Hill County. Big Sandy Creek near Havre crested at 12.07 feet on April 13, which (as of entry) was the fourth highest crest on record. Route 50 was greatly flooded as well as some businesses . Farther north, Lodge Creek below McRae Creek  approached Major Flood stage before cresting at 10.59 feet on April 18th. Much of rural northern Hill County experienced flooding as a result. The Milk River gauge near Havre remained below flood stage, although river levels did come out of their banks farther east, ultimately impacting eastern portions of Havre.
Roads north of Lothair become flooded from snowmelt. Liberty Co law enforcement closed several sections of several roads across the county.

Lewis and Clark County Sheriff's Office reported the high bridge over the Dearborn River was washed out. Public works closed the road at Flat Creek. Several secondary roads across the area were flooded at times. Flooding across northwest Helena also occurred, especially west of Birdseye Road.
Meagher County Sheriff's office stated rockslides were occurring in the Deep Creek Canyon area, affecting Highway 12, due to snowmelt and flooding.

Churchill area saw pretty good runoff occur. Several locations around Amsterdam (Camp and Godfrey Creeks) had water up against houses. The Highline Canal near Gallatin Gateway overtopped in several locations due to runoff.  One house and Axtell Anceny Road were affected. Residents on Dry Creek Road and Swamp Creek Road had flood water around houses.  This caused the evacuation of the Bootstrap Ranch. County Roads had several roads closed with water on them.

Water levels flooded many yards and approached many homes, but no reports of impactful structural flooding were received. Water levels were out of their banks in many areas from Sluice Boxes northward to near Belt.

BTCM8, Belt Creek near Monarch, crested at 6.79 feet on May 17th. Water levels resulted in strong currents that claimed the lives of two men visiting from Canada. The two men went into the fast moving water to retrieve their dog. The dog made it to shore, but the two men were pulled downstream and ultimately drowned. Water levels also flooded a portion of Sluice Boxes State Park's entrance parking lot as well as fields and yards from Sluice Boxes northward to Armington. A house in Neihart was flooded near the area were O'Brien Creek enters Belt Creek.

Water flowed out of the rockier boulder terrain on the east side of the road, crossed the road with water depth being 2 to 3 feet deep at times. Water and debris entered at least two homes. One culvert was completely washed out with drainage pipes unearthed. Some wheat crops were flattened. NWS Employee that lives along the road had water enter their basement. Wilson Butte Road was impassable for approximately an hour.

events.cz_name: GALLATIN AND MADISON COUNTY MOUNTAINS AND CENTENNIAL MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Snotel equipment at Shower Falls estimated 13 inches of new snowfall over a touch less than 36 hours. Given this site is at 8,450 feet elevation, the only impacts were to recreation.

A trained spotter reported 10 inches of total snow on bridges from the event. Additionally, snotel equipment at Many Glacier estimated 10 inches storm total snow. Most snow at the snotel site fell in the morning through afternoon on the 24th.

Snotel equipment at Copper Camp observed the long duration snow event. Through 10AM MDT Wednesday the 25th, 9 inches new snow was estimated. Thereafter, an additional 6 inches of snow fell, totaling 15 inches for the entire event.

A coop observer as well as USFS personnel reported snow accumulations in excess of 6 inches. The coop observer, 4 miles sse of Bynum, measured 6.5 inches new snow by 630 AM MST 10/25. USFS estimated 12 inches new snow in the Augusta area through the early afternoon 10/25.

Several cocorahs volunteer reports and public reports were received of 6 inches storm total snow in the Fairfield and Dutton areas by the morning of 10/25. Additionally, law enforcement reported several slide offs in the Conrad area, where 4 to 5 inches of snow was estimated to have fallen.
Social media report of 6 inches total snow in Fort Benton. Start and end of event are estimated.

events.cz_name: BEARS PAW MOUNTAINS AND SOUTHERN BLAINE
events.event_narrative: A trained spotter reported 10 inches new snow between Tuesday evening and Wednesday afternoon near Hays. Time of reaching impact criteria is estimated. Additionally, law enforcement reported a multi vehicle wreck due to slick roads that resulted in the closure of MT Highway 66 near Hays.

Numerous reports of snow reaching winter storm criteria as well as impacts from the snow were received over this period. Official NWS obs at WFO Great Falls totaled 6 inches new snow for the event. Both an NWS employee and the public reported snowfall amounts in excess of 8 inches around Great Falls. NWS employees on their way in to work saw two jack-knifed semis on Interstate 15 blocking an exit ramp.

events.cz_name: JUDITH BASIN COUNTY AND JUDITH GAP
events.event_narrative: Multiple public reports, trained spotter reports, and an emergency manager reported snowfall totals in excess of 9 inches with this storm. Reports in excess of 9 inches came from Raynesford, the Stanford area, and Hobson The peak amount was measured in Stanford, where 15 inches of storm total snow was measured.

Multiple trained spotters, coop reports, as well as public reports were received for the lower elevations of Fergus county that met winter storm criteria. Reports ranged from up to 13 inches in Lewistown to 12 inches near Hilger, to 15 inches in Grass Range.
Only one report was received in total for this zone. The report came from the public near Marysville, who reported 24 inches storm total snow accumulation. The time of meting criteria is estimated.

Two reports were received that met winter storm criteria in the Gates of the Mountains area. The first was from an NWS employee 6 miles NE of Craig, who measured 9.2 inches storm total snow. Additionally, a coop observer at Holter Dam measured 9 inches new snow for the event.

Three reports of storm total snow of 9 inches or greater were received for the Little Belts. The first report was from SNOTEL equipment at Spur Park, which estimated 9 inches storm total snow. There were two additional public reports, one from Neihart and another from Showdown Montana near Porphyry peak. The storm total reports were 11 and 14 inches respectively.
SNOTEL equipment at Crystal Lake estimated 9 inches new snow by 8 AM the 25th. Snow continued into the late afternoon on the 26th.

Many reports were received from the Helena Valley meeting winter storm criteria. Reports ranged from 6 inches all the way up to 13.4 inches in the Helena area. Official NWS obs at the Helena Airport measured 6.5 inches storm total snow.

Several reports were received of an additional 6 inches of snow in the Helena valley overnight the 25th into the 26th. Most snow fell between midnight and 6 AM in Helena. Official NWS observations at the Helena Airport totaled 6.4 inches late evening the 25th through the early afternoon on the 26th.
Cut Bank Airport ASOS measured a non-thunderstorm wind gust 72 mph. There were other wind gusts observed that met high wind criteria throughout the event.
Trained spotter in White Sulphur Springs reported 12 inches new snow between 6PM 10/24 and 11AM 10/25.

Many sources reported a combination of heavy snow and snow/ice damage, including law enforcement, trained spotters, Snotels, and the public. Multiple wrecks were reported on Homestake Pass by la enforcement the morning of 10/25. Many reports of 9 inches total were received from Montana City, Jefferson City, and Clancy, with a peak snow report of 24 inches in Jefferson City.
A trained spotter reported 12 inches of snow by 10/25 at 8 AM MDT along US-287 in far northwestern Broadwater county. Additionally, the public reported 8 inches of snow in Toston by midday 10/25.
Public reports 7.5 inches new snow 14 miles north northeast of Cardwell along MT-69 by 915 AM 10/25. Start time estimated.

Law enforcement reported one serious injury from a wreck along Interstate 90 near mile marker 262. Law enforcement determined that slick roads from winter weather contributed to the vehicle crash. Additionally, there was a public report of 6 inches new snow 15 miles north of Cardwell along MT-69 between 9 PM 10/25 and 312 PM 10/26.
A co-op observer in Ennis reported 6.7 inches of new snow by 9AM 10/26. Additionally, the public reported 8 inches new snow 12 miles south of Ennis by 10 AM MDT 10/26.

Multiple reports were received in this zone in excess of 6 inches. A co-op observer 1 mile ENE of Sheridan measured 8 inches new snow between 11 PM MDT 10/25 and 7 AM MDT 10/26. Additionally, multiple reports (Trained spotter and public) were received of greater than 6 inches accumulation in Dillon, with the highest total received being 8 inches.

Snow Squall. Starting at 11:15 AM, the precipitation sensor was detected and live webcams showed precipitation increasing from the west. Road surface temperatures were recorded to be between 25 degrees at the start and 23 degrees by 12:30 PM. Wind gusts were between 10 mph and 23 mph from 11:15 AM to 12:30 PM. MDT 15 minute webcam imagery showed near zero visibility between 12 PM and 1 PM. Precipitation sensor stopped reporting activity at 12:45 PM and webcam imagery showed visibility improvement after 1 PM MST.

Snow Squall. Light snow started at the airport at 11:30 AM. Visibility quickly reduced down to 0.75 miles in 9 minutes. ASOS reported winds gusting between 35 and 39 mph. Moderate snow fall by the ASOS was reported between 11:45 and 11:55 AM with visibility down to 0.5 miles. Visibility improved to over 1 mile after 11:55 AM. Airport staff called at 11:45 AM with 0.8 inches of new snow at the airport from the snow squall that passed through and near zero visibility. FAA Webcam 15 minute imagery showed the reduction in visibility of less than a quarter of a mile.

Snow Squall. At 11:35 AM, Three Forks AWOS reported wind speeds sustained at 40 mph and gusts at 52 mph. These conditions continued until 12:15 PM. METAR observation at 12:55 PM reported visibility down to 0.25 miles and haze conditions. FAA webcam imagery between 11:45 AM and 12:30 PM showed snow falling with less than a quarter mile of visibility. Visibility improved to 7 miles at the 1:55 PM METAR observation.
Snow Squall. Visibility less than a quarter of a mile. Heavy snowfall. Blizzard conditions reported by the spotter.

Snow Squall. At 1:20 PM, Bozeman Airport ASOS reported light snow and 40 mph wind gusts with visibility down to 1.25 miles. 4 minutes later, ASOS reported wind gusts up to 44 mph and visibility down to 0.25 miles. These conditions continued for 10 minutes before visibility improved to 0.5 miles, but gusty winds between 30 mph and 45 mph continued for 1 hour. ASOS reported heavy snowfall for 5 minutes, then moderate snow for 10 minutes, then light snow for 20 minutes.

MT DOT sensor at Monarch Canyon showed visibility at or below one-quarter mile for at least 7 hours (Power failed at that point). US-89 was closed from Armington Junction to White Sulphur Springs early morning May 8. The Onion Park Snotel estimated 28 inches new snow with rates of 2 inches per hour. Elsewhere, the Porphyry Peak RAWS reported sustained winds averaging 25 mph, with gusts into the 50's mph before the sensor failed at 1005 PM MDT May 7. A widespread power outage affected much of the zone through Wednesday morning. End time is estimated given lack of observations after late evening of the 7th. The Monarch Fire Department reported 48 inches storm total snow by noon Wednesday the 8th. They reported numerous trees down, trees were on houses, roadways, and in Belt Creek. Other snowfall estimates from snotels in the zone: 29 inches at Stringer Creek over 24 hours, 21 inches at Deadman Creek over 24 hours, and 16 inches of new snow at Spur Park over 24 hours. Two Glacier NP sensors measured gusts in excess of 75 mph, including Logan Pass and Sunpoint. The peak gust observed was at Logan Pass and was 81 mph.
Mesonet stations GW3546, GW0718, and Mt Lebanon SE all measured gusts in excess of 58 mph. The peak observed gust was at GW0718 (25 NNW Joplin) and was 85 mph.
Three sensors measured gusts in excess of 75 mph, including Chouteau South MT DOT, Dellwo DELMT, and Hodgkiss HODMT. The peak gust observed was 85 mph, measured at Chouteau South.
A personal weather device at Upper Elk Creek measured a 72 mph gust. Additionally, the Gleason RAWS GSNM8 measured a 61 mph gust.
AWOS station K1HM Hotel measured a 67 mph gust. MT mesonet sensor at Midway colony measured a 60 mph gust.
Several stations measured criteria gusts, including MTM76 Cascade E (65 mph), MT mesonet sensor Sun River SE (59 mph), ASOS station KGTF Great Falls Airport (63 mph), and FW1843 Great Falls (63 mph).
MT DOT sensor at Flesher Pass measured a 58 mph gust.
Trained spotter reported a 61 mph gust very near Silver City.

events.cz_name: JUDITH BASIN COUNTY AND JUDITH GAP
events.event_narrative: AWOS station K1CM Charlie measured multiple gusts in excess of 58 mph, including a peak of 67 mph. MT DOT sensor Geyser also measured a few gusts in excess of 58 mph, including a peak of 62 mph.
MT DOT sensor at Norris Hill measured a 64 mph gust.
MT Mesonet station Fox Crossing SW measured a 65 mph gust.

events.cz_name: BEARS PAW MOUNTAINS AND SOUTHERN BLAINE
events.event_narrative: RAWS station FBLM8 Fort Belknap Raws measured a 60 mph gust.
AWOS station K1OM Oscar measured a peak gust of 64 mph. MT DOT sensor at Beacon Hill also measured criteria gusts, including a peak of 61 mph.
MT DOT sensors at Monarch Canyon and Kings Hill Pass both measured gusts in excess of 58 mph, including a peak of 66 mph at Monarch Canyon.

events.cz_name: BIG BELT, BRIDGER AND CASTLE MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: MT DOT sensors at Deep Creek Pass and Bridger Canyon measured gusts in excess of 58 mph, including a peak gust of 72 mph at Bridger Canyon.
MT Mesonet station Bowmans Corner measured a 75 mph gust.
MT DOT sensors at Flesher Pass and MacDonald Pass measured gusts in excess of 58 mph, including a peak gust of 62 mph at MacDonald Pass.
A trained spotter near Silver City reported a 73 mph gust. MT DOT sensor at Sieben Flats also measured two gusts in excess of 58 mph.
ASOS station KHLN Helena Airport measured two gust sin excess of 58 mph, including a peak of 64 mph.
MT DOT sensor at Norris Hill measured a few 59 mph gusts in addition to a two hour period of sustained winds averaging 43 mph.

Mesonet station MTM76 Cascade E, MT Mesonet station Sun River SE, official NWS Great Falls obs (RSOIS), and ASOS station KGTF Great Falls Airport all measured wind gusts of 58 mph of or greater, including a peak gust of 63 mph at Cascade E and Sun River SE.
Chinook COOP CNKM8 observed 24 hour snowfall of 8 inches between 9pm Thursday and 9pm Friday.
Social media reported 6.3 inches of snow in Cascade. Spotters reported a storm total of 8 inches near Ulm and 6 inches at the Great Falls NWS office.
A storm spotter 5 miles NE of Hilger reported a 24 hour snowfall total of 8 inches.
A spotter 6 miles north of Bozeman reported 6 inches of storm total snow. Observers in Bozeman reported 7 to 8 inches of snow.
Social media reported 10 inches of snow in Highwood.

events.cz_name: BEARS PAW MOUNTAINS AND SOUTHERN BLAINE
events.event_narrative: Trained spotter 9 SW Chinook reported 8 inches new snow during the day on the 12th, ending at the report time. Start and criteria time are estimated.
Social media report of one quarter of an inch of ice accrual between Townsend and Deep Creek Pass.
Trained spotter 5 NNE Loma reports 7 inches new snow in total by the report time. Snow was heavy at the time of the report but we never received a follow-up report with a final total.

events.cz_name: JUDITH BASIN COUNTY AND JUDITH GAP
events.event_narrative: A coop observer in Stanford and the public near Buffalo observed snow in excess of 6 inches, with the highest amount (8 inches) near Buffalo. Start time is estimated.

Multiple reports, including from trained spotters and coop observers, reported storm total snow in excess of 6 inches. The peak reports were from Lewistown as well as Grass Range, which were both at a foot.
Official NWS obs at the Havre Airport, in addition to multiple public reports, reported snow in excess of 6 inches. The peak report was from 15 N Rudyard and was 10 inches.
A report from the public was received that stated 7 inches of snow fell in Chinook on the 12th. Start, criteria, and end times are all estimated.
A coop observer in Chinook measured storm total snow of 8.9 inches over two reports. The start, criteria, and end times are estimated.

RAWS station SRYM8 Saint Mary measured a 59 mph gust.
Mesonet station SNPMT Sunpoint measured a 75 mph wind gust. Mesonet station LGPVC Logan Pass (GNP) also measured high wind gusts.
Mesonet Site DOGM8 Dog Gun Lake MT measured an 81 mph wind gust. Mesonet station MTBRN Two Medicine Bridge (MT DOT) also measured a high wind gust.

Wunderground sensor KMTLEWIS74 reported a 66 mph wind gust.

events.event_narrative: Mesonet station MTBDC Bridger Canyon Mt measured a 61 mph wind gust.

Mesonet stations MTCHK Chinook and MTM48 Chinook E MDA both measured gusts in excess of 58 mph, in addition to MTCHK measuring sustained winds averaging 40 mph over an hour. The peak observed gust was 63 mph at Chinook E MDA.

events.cz_name: BEARS PAW MOUNTAINS AND SOUTHERN BLAINE
events.event_narrative: MT mesonet station Cleveland N and RAWS station FBLM8 Fort Belknap both measured gusts in excess of 58 mph, in addition to Cleveland N measuring sustained winds averaging at least 40 mph over an hour. The peak observed gust was at Cleveland N and was 71 mph. There was also a report received of a tin roof being ripped off a shed and thrown between 150 and 200 feet downwind.

ASOS station KGTF Great Falls Airport, AWOS station K1AM Raynesford, MTM76 Cascade E MDA, and MT mesonet stations Eden NW and Sun River SE all measured gusts of 58 mph or greater, with Sun River SE measuring sustained winds of 40 mph or greater over at least an hour. The peak observed gust was 64 mph at Sun River SE.
Mesonet station MTMON Monarch Canyon and RAWS station SFJM8 South Fork Judith measured gusts in excess of 58 mph, including a peak gust of 63 mph at Monarch Canyon.

MT mesonet stations Carter N, Highwood Bench, Frenchmans Ridge, Fort Benton E, and MTM02 S Loma, along with mesonet station MTLOM Loma DOT all measured gusts in excess of 58 mph, including a few reports of sustained winds of 40 mph averaged over an hour. The peak observed gust was 61 mph at several sensors.

A combination of mesonet sensors (Forestgrove N and MTBCH Beacon Hill) and AWOS sensors (KMVH N Bar Ranch, K1OM Oscar, and K1NM November) all measured gusts of 58 mph or greater. The peak observed gust was 75 mph at Beacon Hill.

An ambient weather station, RAWS station SRYM8 Saint Mary RAWS, and mesonet station SNPMT Sunpoint in Glacier NP measured gusts in excess of 60 mph, including a peak gust of 67 mph at the Ambient station in Babb.

Multiple sensors in this zone, including MTBRN Two Medicine Bridge, MT Mesonet stations Dog Gun Lake E, Wetzel NE, and Dupuyer N, and MTBWG Browning DOT measured gusts in excess of 75 mph or sustained winds averaging 50 mph or greater over at least an hour. The peak observed gust was 94 mph at the Browning DOT sensor.

events.cz_name: EASTERN GLACIER, WESTERN TOOLE, AND CENTRAL PONDERA
events.event_narrative: Numerous sensors in this zone reported sustained winds of 40 mph or greater observed over at least an hour or gusts to 58 mph or greater, including MT mesonet stations Mission Lake S, Buffalo Lake E, Sunburst NNW, Conrad N, Ledger N MDA, and Ethridge N, MT DOT sensors Sunburst (MTSUN), Sweet Grass (MTSWT), and Valier Jct (MTVAR), and ASOS/AWOS stations KCTB Cut Bank and KSBX Shelby. There were more sensors than this, but you get the point. Peak observed gust in this zone was 84 mph at Mission Lake S.
Mesonet stations MTM51 Gildford and MTM06 N Havre both measured gusts of 58 mph or greater, including a peak gust of 60 mph at Gildford.

events.cz_name: JUDITH BASIN COUNTY AND JUDITH GAP
events.event_narrative: Mesonet station MTGYS Geyser, AWOS station K1CM Charlie, and MT mesonet stations Judith Gap, Moccasin, and Benchland all measured gusts of 58 mph or greater. The peak gust was at Geyser, and was 67 mph.
A personal weather station at Upper Elk Creek, RAWS station GSNM8 Gleason, and MT DOT sensor MTROG Rogers Pass measured gusts in excess of 60 mph, including a peak gust of 82 mph at Upper Elk Creek.

Many sensors in this zone measured sustained winds of 50 mph or greater over at least an hour or gusts in excess of 75 mph, including sensors MTCTS Choteau South, DELMT Dellwo, MTPND Pendroy, and Bynum W MT mesonet. The peak observed gust at a sensor was 88 mph at Dellwo along the immediate eastern slopes of the Rockies.
Mesonet station Mtfps Flesher Pass MTDOT measured a 59 mph gust.

Numerous sensors in northern Liberty measured strong winds and gusts, including GW0718 Joplin 25 NNW and MT mesonet station Mt Lebanon SE to name a couple. The peak observed gusts was 82 mph at Joplin 25 NNW.
Mesonet station MTNOR Norris Hill measured several instances of high sustained winds, in addition to a few gusts in excess of 58 mph. The peak gust at this sensor was 61 mph.
Mesonet station MTM73 Ledger N MDA measured two gusts of 58 mph or greater, including a peak gust of 63 mph.

RAWS station WRSM8 and mesonet station MTBHP Big Hole Pass (MT DOT) measured gusts at or in excess of 58 mph, including a peak gust of 74 mph at Wise River. Big Hole Pass also measured sustained winds, averaging 41 mph, from 931AM MST through 335 PM MST.

ASOS station KDLN measured multiple gusts in excess of 58 mph, including a peak gust of 97 mph at 931 AM. Power to the ASOS and surrounding community was lost as this peak gust occurred, resulting in limited observations elsewhere. Two other reports were received from the Dillon area stating that a large tree was uprooted and that the wind caused a greenhouse to collapse.

events.cz_name: RUBY MOUNTAINS AND SOUTHERN BEAVERHEAD MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Several RAWS stations, including HRKM8 Harkness, LMRM8 Antelope, and BRRM8 Brenner in addition to mesonet station MTMQM Monida Pass (MT DOT) measured gusts in excess of 60 mph. The peak observed gust was 68 mph at Brenner.

events.cz_name: GALLATIN AND MADISON COUNTY MOUNTAINS AND CENTENNIAL MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Multiple sensors in this zone measured strong winds and gusts at lower elevations (Not at the high peaks), including MTBSK Big Sky Road (MT DOT), RAWS stations RRDM8 Red Rock and BTKM8 Burnt Creek, and NW Energy sensors Cornucopia Rd near Virginia City. The peak observed gust was at Cornucopia Rd and was 76 mph.

Multiple sensors across Northern Blaine county (including the US-2 corridor), measured gusts in excess of 58 mph or sustained winds, averaging 40 mph over at least an hour. These sensors include MTCHK Chinook US-2 mp 403.5 (MT DOT), BFTM 4.4 E Hogeland (Agrimet), MT mesonet sensor Savoy SW, AWOS station S719 Chinook, MT mesonet sensor Hogeland SW, and MT mesonet sensor Turner N. The peak observed gust was at Savoy SW (9 miles ESE of Fort Belknap) and was 82 mph. Sustained winds averaging 50 mph, averaged over an hour, were observed north of US-2 near Turner and Hogeland.

events.cz_name: BEARS PAW MOUNTAINS AND SOUTHERN BLAINE
events.event_narrative: Numerous sensors in this zone measured sustained winds of 40 mph or greater averaged over at least an hour, or gusts of 58 mph or greater, including RAWS station FBLM8 Fort Belknap and LBCM8 Little Bullwhacker Creek, Montana mesonet stations Dry Lake, Cleveland N, Warrick S, and Big Sandy SE. An additional public report was received stating gusts similar to what these sensors observed. The peak observed gust in this zone was observed on the Fort Belknap reservation at the Fort Belknap RAWS (88 mph) between 618 PM and 718 PM.

A few sensors in this zone measured gusts of 58 mph or greater or sustaiend winds of 40 mph or greater averaged over at least an hour, including RAWS stations EKHM8 Elkhorn and GAAM8 Galena, and mesonet stations MTSPK Spokane Creek (MT DOT) and MTCLN Clancy (MT DOT). Public reports were also received from Montana City and Clancyof pine trees down blocking roadways. THe peak observed gust was at Spokane Creek (75 mph).

Several sensors measured sustained winds of 40 mph or greater averaged over at least an hour or gusts of 58 mph or greater, including RAWS station GINM8 Ginger, Montana mesonet station Toston, Agrimet station TOSM 5.5 SW Toston, and mesonet station MTTOS Toston Bridge US-287 (MT DOT). The peak observed gust was at the Ginger RAWS (85 mph).

A few sensors measured gusts in excess of 58 mph or sustained winds of 40 mph averaged over at last an hour, including RAWS station SFJM8 South Fork Judith, and mesonet station MTMON Monarch Canyon (MT DOT), and MTKIH Kings Hill Pass (MT DOT). The peak gust observed was 74 mph at South Fork Judith RAWS.

Many sensors measured gusts of 58 mph or greater or sustained winds of 40 mph or greater averaged over at least an hour, including Montana mesonet stations Belt NW, Sun River SE, Benton Lake W, and Eden NW, ASOS/AWOS stations KGTF Great Falls Airport, K1IM India, K1AM Alpha, and KGFA Malmstrom Air Force Base, as well as mesonet stations FW1843 Great Falls (10 WSW Stockett) and FW5493 Vaughn (1 WSW Sun Prairie). TH epeak observed gust was 75 mph at the Belt NW Montana mesonet station.

Numerous sensors in this zone measured gusts of 58 mph or greater or sustained winds of 40 mph or greater averaged over at least an hour, including Montana mesonet stations Carter N, Big Sandy SW, Highwood Bench, Big Sandy NW, and Frenchman Ridge, AWOS station K79S Fort Benton Airport, mesonet stations MTLOM Loma (MT DOT), GW6710 Meadowlane, GW6518 Big Sandy Airport, and GW3862 Loma 18 NW. The peak observed gust was 85 at Montana Mesonet station Carter N.

Numerous sensors in this zone measured sustained winds of 40 mph or greater averaged over at least an hour or gust of 58 mph or greater, including Montana mesonet sensors Coffee Creek N, Christina W, Forestgrove N, Roy E, and Winifred NE, AWOS/ASOS sensors KLWT Lewistown Airport, K1EM Echo, K1OM Oscar, K1NM November, KMVH N Bar Ranch, and K1DM Delta, mesonet sensors MTDEN Denton (MT DOT), MTBOH Bohemian Corner (MT DOT), MTBCH Beacon Hill (MT DOT), and RAWS sensor ARMM8 Armells Creek. Public reports were received of shingles blown off of roofs, in addition to power going in and out all day near Denton. The peak gust in this zone was 87 mph at Beacon Hill in SE Fergus county. Of particular note, sustained winds averaged 53 mph at Beacon Hill between 145 PM 12/17 and 1 AM 12/18.

This zone does not have many sensors, so verification is a bit sparse. The one DOT sensor at Lewistown Divide lost power and did not report winds/gusts for the overwhelming majority of the event. The other reliable sensor is Judith Peak RAWS JPKM8, though that sensor is at a mountain peak. Given these factors, the source for this verification is a single Ambient Weather sensor which measured a 59 mph gust southeast of Lewistown. If you were to include Judith Peak, the peak observed gust in this zone was 94 mph and the duration of the event would expand through much of the day December 17.

events.cz_name: JUDITH BASIN COUNTY AND JUDITH GAP
events.event_narrative: Quite a few sensors measured sustained winds of 40 mph or greater averaged over at least an hour or gusts of 58 mph or greater, including mesonet stations MTEDD Eddies Corner (MT DOT), MTGYS Geyser (MT DOT), MWSM 2 W Moccasin, AWOS station K1CM Charlie, and Montana mesonet stations Moccasin and Judith Gap. The peak gust of the day was observed at Judith Gap (84 mph).

Several sources reported sustained winds of 40 mph averaged over at least an hour or gusts of 58 mph, including ASOS station KBZN Bozeman Airport, Montana mesonet station Manhattan S, mesonet station AV387 Manhattan, as well as trained spotters. The peak gust in the Gallatin valley was reported by a trained spotter 1 NW of Amsterdam, who measured a 78 mph gust. Additional damage reports include 100-foot pine trees being snapped and blown over and portions of 8-feet fences being blown away completely.

events.cz_name: BIG BELT, BRIDGER AND CASTLE MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Quite a few sensors in this zone measured sustained winds of 40 mph or greater, averaged over at least an hour, or gusts of 58 mph or greater, including mesonet sensors MTBDC Bridger Canyon (MT DOT), MTBZH Bozeman Pass (MT DOT), and MTDPC Deep Creek Pass (MT DOT), as well as RAWS station TT838 Battle Ridge. The peak gust observed was 84 mph at Bozeman Pass along Interstate 90.

Multiple sensors measured sustained winds of 50 mph or greater averaged over at least an hour, or gusts in excess of 75 mph, including Montana mesonet stations Dog Gun Lake E, Wetzel NE, and Dupuyer N, mesonet stations MTBWG Browning (MT DOT), SHBM Browning, MTBRN Two Medicine Bridge (MT DOT), and RAWS station BGRM8 Browning. The peak observed gust in this zone was 95 mph at Dog Gun Lake E. This sensor also recorded sustained winds, averaged over an hour, of 68 mph between 1205 PM and 105 PM MST.

events.cz_name: EASTERN GLACIER, WESTERN TOOLE, AND CENTRAL PONDERA
events.event_narrative: Numerous sensors reported sustained winds of 40 mph or greater averaged over at least an hour, or gusts of 58 mph or greater, including Montana mesonet stations Mission Lake S, Buffalo Lake E, Ethridge N, Sunburst NW, and Conrad N, ASOS station KCTB Cut Bank Airport, AWOS station KSBX Shelby Airport, mesonet stations BFAM 12 W Cut Bank, MTVAR Valier Junction I-15 (MT DOT), GW1987 Ethridge 3 SE, MTSUN Sunburst (MT DOT), GW0664 Shelby Airport, DW0975 Kevin, MTSWT Sweet Grass (MT DOT), and FW8513 Sunburst. The peak observed gust was 88 mph at Mission Lake S. Several instances of sustained winds averaging 50 mph over at least an hour were observed along Interstate 15.

Two Ambient stations measured gusts in excess of 60 mph, including ambient station Howards Lodge in Babb and Glacier Park Trading Company in East Glacier Park. The peak gust observed was at Howards Lodge (72 mph).

Numerous sensors in Hill County measured sustained winds of 40 mph or greater averaged over at least an hour or gusts of 58 mph or greater, including mesonet sensors EW1937 Goldstone, GW3530 Rudyard 11 S, GW4079 Inverness 10 SSE, MTINV Inverness (MT DOT), EW1931 Rudyard, FW1664 Hingham, MTM06 ARC N Havre, GW6391 Gildford 10 N, GW6390 Gildford 6 SE, and GW6392 Gildford 15 N, ASOS station KHVR Havre Airport, and Montana mesonet stations Fox Crossing SW, Lake Thibadeau W, Simpson, Kremlin NW, Inverness S,  and Inverness N. The peak gust of 79 mph was observed at Fox Crossing. Some stations lost power through the event, so the peak gust may have been stronger. Sustained winds at Fox Crossing averaged 59 mph over an hour between 345 and 445 PM MST.

MT DOT sensor MTBLS Boulder South MT-69 mp 27.7 measured multiple gusts of greater than 58 mph in addition to a period of high sustained winds (42 mph averaged over an hour). The peak gust was 71 mph.

Montana mesonet site DOGM8 Dog Gun Lake had an average sustained wind speed of 52 mph from 12:25 to 14:15 MST and measured high wind gusts.  Mesonet station MTBWG Browning (MT DOT), and Wetzel NE also measured high sustained winds and wind gusts.

events.cz_name: EASTERN GLACIER, WESTERN TOOLE, AND CENTRAL PONDERA

Mt Lebanon SE Montana Mesonet site averaged a sustained wind of 41 mph from 4:10 PM until 5:35 PM MST. This site also measured a 65 mph wind gust.

Mesonet site DOGM8 Dog Gun Lake measured an average sustained wind of 50 mph from 5:15 PM to 6:15 PM MST.
Mesonet station SNPMT Sunpoint measured a high wind gust. Mesonet station LGPVC Logan Pass (GNP) and Mesonet station SRYM8 Saint Mary RAWS also had a high wind gust.

Mesonet station MTBRN Two Medicine Bridge (MT DOT) measured an 89 mph wind gust and measured an average high sustained wind of 60 mph on the 12th between 9:00 AM and 11:00 AM MST. A few other stations measured high wind gusts and sustained winds during the period.

events.cz_name: EASTERN GLACIER, WESTERN TOOLE, AND CENTRAL PONDERA

Mesonet station GSNM8 Gleason RAWS measured a 61 mph wind gust.
Mesonet station DELMT Dellwo (MCSCN) measured a 63 mph wind gust. A few other weather stations also measured high wind gusts during this period.
Mesonet station MTM02 10.2 S Loma (MT-MESO) measured a 60 mph wind gust. Mesonet station MTLOM Loma (MT DOT) also measured a high wind gust.
ASOS station KGTF Great Falls Airport measured a 64 mph wind gust. Multiple weather stations also hit a high wind gust.

events.cz_name: JUDITH BASIN COUNTY AND JUDITH GAP
events.event_narrative: Mesonet station MTGYS Geyser (MT DOT) measured a 71 mph wind gust. AWOS station K1CM Charlie also measured a high wind gust.
Mesonet station Forestgrove N observed an average 41 mph sustained winds between 12:15 PM and 1:15 PM MST.
Mesonet station MTFPS Flesher Pass S-279 Mp 30.5 measured a 69 mph wind gust.
Montana mesonet site Mt Lebanon SE measured a 68 mph wind gust. Mesonet site GW3546 Whitlash also measured a 40 mph average sustained wind over the span of an hour.

Numerous sensors in this zone measured sustained winds averaged over at least an hour of 50 mph, or gusts in excess of 75 mph. These sensors include mesonet stations MTM49 7 NE Choteau, DELMT Dellwo, MTCTS Choteau South US-287 (MT DOT), MTPND Pendroy (MT DOT), RICMT Rice Ridge, MCBMT McBranty, TRFM Teton River Agrimet, HODMT Hodgkiss, DAHMT Dahlman, GOLMT Gollehan, and MTBOW Bowmans Corner (MT DOT), AWOS stations K1GM Golf and K1FM Foxtrot, Montana mesonet stations Bynum W, Augusta N, and Bowmans Corner. A co-op observer near Bynum reported roof damage and mailboxes being blown away. The peak gust observed was 104 mph at Bynum W Montana mesonet. Sustained winds at Bynum W averaged 74 mph between 1250 PM and 150 PM MST.
Montana Mesonet site Turner N measured an average sustained wind of 41 mph from 6:15 P.M. until 10:00 P.M. MST. Mesonet site Hogeland HOGM8 also measured a high wind gust.

events.cz_name: JUDITH BASIN COUNTY AND JUDITH GAP
events.event_narrative: Montana mesonet site Judith Gap had an average sustained wind speed of 41 mph from 10:55 to 11:55 A.M MST. Mesonet site Eddies Corner MTEDD measured a 59 mph wind gust.
Montana mesonet site Coffee Creek N measured a 65 mph wind gust. Montana mesonet site Forestgrove, MTBCH Beacon Hill, and AWOS station KMVH N Bar Ranch also measured a high wind gust.

Two MDT sensors (Flesher Pass and MacDonald Pass) and a NW Energy sensor (002NW Hwy 12 measured gusts in excess of 58 mph, including a peak gust of 78 mph at Flesher Pass. The sensor at MacDonald Pass measured sustained winds of 44 mph between 1145 AM and 715PM. At the NW energy sensor Hwy 12, sustained winds averaged 40 mph between 320 PM and 420 PM. Finally, a public report was received stating 26 trees were blown down across Stemple Pass Rd 10 miles ESE of Lincoln.

Numerous sensors and a trained spotter reported gusts in excess of 58 mph or sustained winds averaging at least 40 mph over an hour or more, including mesonet station MTSBN Sieben Flats (MT DOT), RAWS station DBOM8 Dearborn and NW Energy sensor Birdseye Rd. The peak gust reported was from the trained spotter 7 miles east of Marysville, which was 80 mph. The trained spotter also reported a 40 foot tall pine tree was toppled due to the winds. Additionally, the Sieben Flats sensor measured sustained winds averaging 41 mph between 931AM and 234 PM, at which time the sensor lost power and stopped reporting. The last observation at this sensor before reporting stopped was sustained winds of 60 mph with a gust to 79 mph.

Wunderground sensor Upper Elk Creek (KMTAUGUS3) Measured a 71 mph gust. While this does not satisfy the typical higher criteria of 75 mph for this zone, the overwhelming pile of evidence supporting a high-end wind day in addition the fact that there are no Windy sensors in this zone leaves very little options. It was incredibly windy but there were no sensors in areas that were not protected from winds at least in some capacity.

Numerous sensors measured high winds and numerous reports of damage were received from trained spotters and the public. Sensors that reported criteria winds: ASOS station KHLN Helena Airport, mesonet station HVMT Helena Agrimet, HRWM8 Helena RAWS, and mesonet station FW7359 Helena. The peak observed gust was 91 mph at the Helena Airport ASOS. Power was lost at the Helena Airport when this gust occurred. Due to the power outage the extend of 5 minute data was lost, bur prior to this 91 mph gust, sustained winds averaged 42 mph between 1035 AM and 2 PM. ||As for reports received from trained spotters and the public: 1 mile SE of Helena there was a report of a traffic sign bent over with debris blowing through the streets. Several reports were received stating large trees were down across the valley. 4 miles ENE or Helena there was a report of a horse shelter being destroyed. A more comprehensive tree damage report was received from Helena stating the top third of 50-60 ft conifers were snapped off, power poles broke, and roof tiles were coming off of buildings. ||KTVH posted a video interviewing Helena Parks, which stated there were greater than 1,000 trees down across city limits, and that each tree was approximately $450 to address. Additionally, trees weakened that are still standing will still have to be addressed later in the spring, adding even most cost to the cleanup activities. The video estimated a cost between $25,000 and $30,000 for the cleanup, not including any private property damaged. Given there is additional cleanup necessary later this spring, and that there is likely no way to get a final estimate for damages combining public and private damage, the cost will be left as unknown at this time.||Additional Impacts: Helena Public Schools implemented an early release and activated emergency protocol for students traveling home. Several images were received showing a metal light post being bent all the way to the ground. Severe driving conditions were reported by 511MT along Interstate 15 through the Helena Valley due to exceedingly strong cross winds and numerous tipped semis.

Numerous sensors measured gusts of 58 mph or greater or sustained winds of 40 mph or greater averaged over at least an hour. The quantity of sensors is too many to list, but here are a few that had notable gusts: Montana Mesonet station Mt Lebanon SE (94 mph), mesonet station GW3478 TCTIBER (80 mph), and mesonet station GW3546 Whitlash 7 South (91 mph).

Mesonet station MTNOR Norris Hill (MT DOT) measured a 59 mph gust and high sustained winds of 44 mph, averaged over 2.5 hours. Additionally, AWOS station KEKS Ennis Airport measured sustained winds, averaged over an hour and 40 minutes, of 41 mph.
A wunderground sensor at IngerRanch 5 WSW of Martinsdale measured a gust of 86 mph. Additionally, a trained spotter reported a 67 mph gust 1 mile SW of White Sulphur Springs.

Quite a few sensors measured gusts of 58 mph or greater or sustained winds of 40 mph or greater averaged over at least an hour. These sensors include mesonet station MTM54 SW Power, MTTRV Teton River (MT DOT), AWOS stations K1HM Hotel and K1JM Juliett, mesonet station DAHMT Dahlman, and Montana mesonet stations Brady NE and Midway Colony. The peak gust was 78 mph and was observed at the Midway Colony.

The Rock Ridge Fire was first reported around 2:10pm MST on March 8th 4 miles south of Geraldine. High winds quickly burned 700 acres of grassland by the evening. Containment/end time was estimated. Unknown damages to structures reported.

The Eldorado fire started about 7 miles north of Choteau on the 8th during the afternoon. High winds in the area quickly burned through grassland and shrub, and also jumped over U.S Highway 89. The fire grew to 500 acres and U.S. Highway 89 MM 55 to 63 was briefly closed. The fire became fully contained later in the evening. Damages were reported to cattle rangeland, planted winter wheat, and farm fencing.

The Vegetation Fire started during the afternoon of the 17th about 5 miles west of Gallatin Gateway. This fire burned 600 acres before ending late that night. No known damages were reported from the fire.

The Panama fire started during the afternoon on March 18th, just to the north of mile marker 263 of I-90 near Cardwell. The fire burned through 598 acres before becoming fully contained in the afternoon of March 20th. No known damages were reported due to the fire.

A human-caused wildfire began to burn in the Scratchgravel hills of the West Central Helena Valley when a prescribed burn ember reignited causing a new fire to develop.

The Stonewall Fire was ignited by lightning from a thunderstorm that came through the area at about 3 p.m. on Monday, August 27. The fire burned about 12 acres in heavy, dense timber in the Helena National Forest-Lincoln Ranger District, about one mile south of the Stonewall Lookout and about five miles north of the town of Lincoln, Montana. Smoke was visible from Highway 200. The fire may continue to smolder for a period of time but is considered 100% contained.
The East Fork Fire was reported on August 22, 2012 and was caused by lightning from thunderstorms that went through the Lincoln area on Tuesday, August 21st.
There were five fires in the Lincoln Ranger District. All five of these wildfires were sparked by lightning that moved through the Lincoln area Saturday evening, October 1, 2011.
The Elbow Pass Complex is a wildfire group comprised of five different lightning ignitions from July 12 through July 31, 2012.

The skier was a 32 year old male from Bozeman that had been skiing out of bounds north of Bridger Bowl in what is called the Barney Avalanche Slide Path. The skier caused the avalanche at the ridge breaking a large cornice free and landed approximately 450 yards down the hill. The skier was able to dig his way out of the snow. The Reynolds Creek Fire began around 3:45 pm on Tuesday, July 21. It was in an area approximately six miles east of Logan Pass and four miles west of the Saint Mary Visitor Center. The fire burned thousands of trees along Going-to-the-Sun Road, two structures were lost, including the historic Baring Creek Cabin and an old homestead along Saint Mary Lake that was constructed prior to the creation of the park. A vehicle was also destroyed in the fire. The cost of the fire was approximately 10.1 million as of August 7, 2015 and the cause of the fire is under investigation.

At approximately 4 pm MDT, the Birdseye Wildfire broke out on the north side of Helena and grew to about 613 acres. Red Flag conditions preceded the fire start, with westerly gusting near 40 mph and relative humidity near 15%. A slightly cooler and more humid air mass moved in around 5 pm MDT as winds shifted to the north and eventually diminished.  Evacuations were ordered for areas south of Lincoln Rd, west of Green Meadow and north of Custer but were lifted after 830 pm MDT according to local media. No injuries, fatalities, or property damage was reported with this fire.

A lightning hold out fire was discovered in the foothills northeast of Bozeman when dry conditions began to feed its growth. the fire was initially only able to grow to about 400 acres but then exploded to 7000 acres the next day as red flag conditions moved into the region. At one point, the fire was classified as a type 1 incident and eventually grew to 8224 acres. The fire persisted through mid- October and destroyed 68 structures, including 30 residential homes. It caused damage to 11 structures, of which five were residences. The containment cost was $7.225 million.

The Goose Fire was located near Hoodoo Pass about 32 miles south of Ennis. The fire was  ignited by lightning on July 1st and burned through the month of July, though it was 80 percent contained by August 1st. The initial 250 acre fire was inaccessible to containment crews and was classified as a type 2 incident during its peak on July 10th. By the end of the month, it grew to 7,522 acres and at one structure was destroyed. The cost to fight the fire was about $7.6 million.

The Balsinger Fire is located near Neihart, MT and was ignited by lightning. It became a part of the Divide Complex type one incident team on July 23rd.  Pre-evacuation notices were given to the residents of the northern Belt Creek Drainage area and the town of Monarch on Sunday July 25th. The fire grew to 8511 acres by the end of the month.

The Ellis Fire was discovered in the Helena National Forest about 2.5 miles southwest of the Smith River on July 8th. It became a part of the Divide Complex type one incident team on July 23rd, and the cause is still under investigation. The fire had burned 1,227 acres by the end of the month.

The Alder Creek Fire was discovered in the north Pioneer Mountains just north of Wise River on July 8th. This fire grew to 10,300 acres and its containment effort became a top national priority as it was in close proximity to 239 homes and the Wise River Scenic Byway. It became a part of a type one incident team, which included several other fires in southwest Montana. The cause of the fire is still unknown.

The Trailside Fire was a lightning caused fire discovered near highway 43 in far northwest Beaverhead county on July 8th. The fire grew to over 31,100 acres by the end of the month and resulted the closures of numerous campgrounds, though highway 43 remained open.

The Rock Creek Fire was discovered near mile marker 232 on interstate 15 on July, 10th, and its cause is still unknown.  The fire grew to 3,420 acres and resulted in at least a several hour closure of interstate 15 between Craig and Wolf Creek, along with a few other local road closures. The fire was 100 percent contained on July 14th.

The Woods Creek Fire was lightning caused fire located in the Big Belt Mountains, discovered on July 10th. It was classified as a type one incident on July 31st, and resulted in evacuations on the eastern side of the fire. It ultimately burned 55,449 acres with an estimated incident cost of $27,000,000, as of January 2022.

The Woods Creek Fire began on June 13th when a fallen tree caused a downed power line. Over the course of the fire, three single-family homes were destroyed, along with four other structures. In addition, a Montana DNRC helicopter fighting the fire crash-landed, causing it to catch on fire. All five people on board survived the crash with minor injuries. Total cost of fighting the fire was estimated to be $5.8 million USD as of January 2022. An estimated 4,648 acres burned.

The Dry cabin Fire was a lightning caused incident located in the Scapegoat/Bob Marshall Wilderness area northwest of Lincoln. Steep terrain and heavy fuels allowed this fire to quickly grow in size and become a long term incident and was being managed by a type 3 team by the end of July. The fire size was 3,000 acres and was zero percent contained, but no structures were lost due to it's remote location.

The Christensen Fire was discovered on July 16th in the Beaverhead/Deer Lodge National Forest. The fire grew to 5,442 acres and was zero percent contained on July 31st. The fire was located near the high profile Trailside and Alder Creek Fires.

The American Fork Fire was a lightning caused incident located in the Crazy Mountains. Only the northwest flank of this fire was located in Meagher County, with a majority of it residing over Park and  Sweet Grass Counties. By July 31st, the fire charred 14,397 acres and was only 10 percent contained at that time. This fire merged with the Ohearn Creek Fire on July 18th, 2021. At one point it became a part of the Divide Complex type 1 team managed by the Southern Area Incident Management team.

The Harris Mountain Fire was a lightning caused fire discovered on July, 23rd. Gusty westerly winds and rugged terrain propelled the fire's burn area to 3,000 acres in less than one day. It prompted the evacuation of about 60 residents just a couple days after its discovery and was being managed by a type two incident team at that point. The fire ultimately burned 31,603. Estimated incident cost was $9,770,000.

The lightning caused Black Mountain Fire was discovered on July 17th and grew to 1,021 acres by the end of the month. It was eventually managed by a type one incident team, along with the Alder and Trail Creek Fires, though its impacts were less than those major incidents.

The Crown Mountain Fire started within the Forest boundary of the Helena-Lewis and Clark National Forest some 15 miles southwest of Augusta, MT. During the initial three days, gusty winds, unseasonably high temperatures, and dry conditions resulted in active fire behavior and dangerous firefighting conditions for direct attack on the fire. These circumstances forced air and ground crews to disengage from the fire on 10/5 and 10/6. The fire is burning within portions of the footprint of the 1988 Canyon Creek Fire. The containment withstood winds exceeding 50mph on 10/9 and 10/10 ahead of a cold front that moved in. From 10/11 until present cooler conditions have prevailed with 2 inches of snow falling on the fire area on 10/12. |As of mid-November, the fire was 30% contained and had burned nearly 1,400 acres.

The South Moccasin Fire began on October 4, 2021 around 12:45, and quickly grew in size over the course of the afternoon in unseasonably warm, dry, and breezy conditions. This fire would quickly consume a large portion of the South Moccasin range, along with 5 structures (these were not primary residences). The NWR transmitter for Lewistown sustained some damage, but remained operational.

The Haystack Fire was a lightning caused incident first discovered on July 31st, 2021. It was a relatively quiet event until September 18th, when strong southwesterly winds and critically low relative humidity fueled its growth to 10,800 acres. This led to pre-evacuation notice being issued for the Depot Hill and Boulder hot Springs area, according to KRTV.

The West Wind Fire was first reported on Tuesday, November 30, 2021 as a start in Judith Basin County that quickly spread into Fergus County. High winds with gusts over 60 mph pushed the fire into the town of Denton, MT where multiple structures were threatened. 25 primary structures, 18 secondary structures and 6 commercial structures are destroyed, along with 100,000 bushels of recently harvested grain that burned in two grain elevators. The fire was caused by a powerline.

A wildfire began on the south side of Great Falls early in the morning of December 1st as the result of arson. This fire quickly grew with winds gusting to 50-60 mph, and spread into the Gibson Flats neighborhood, where it caused up to 65 people to be evacuated from their homes, and would ultimately burn 11 homes, 7 garages, and 11 outbuildings as the fire burned 112 acres before it was able to be contained. To date, this is Great Fall's most destructive wild fire.

A grass fire near Blackfoot, Montana was reported at 4:22 am on December 1st, fueled by dry grasses and wind gusts over 90 mph. Despite these strong winds and dry grasses, fire officials were able to control the fire by 11am, allowing residents to return to their homes. No homes were lost to the blaze, but a barn was damaged as the fire burned 780 acres.
